summary: This informational memo describes problems of using Mobile IPv4 in networks that connect to the Internet through a VPN gateway, since they lack well-described solutions. It illustrates the problems and proposes guidelines for possible solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile IP lets a laptop keep its connection while it moves between networks, and a VPN keeps a company's internal network unreachable from outside. RFC 4093 shows that the two do not currently fit together: a roaming user has to encrypt the Mobile IP signalling to reach the corporate network, and the equipment in between cannot read encrypted packets. It then lists what any fix would have to satisfy.

subtitle: Why a roaming Mobile IP user cannot get through a corporate VPN gateway, and what a fix has to satisfy.

tldr.problem: A mobile node that has to reach its home agent through a corporate VPN gateway has to encrypt its Mobile IP traffic, and the machines in the path then cannot read it, so registration fails or the tunnel has to be rebuilt on every handoff.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out five deployment scenarios, works through the two ways the roaming breaks, and then lists ten guidelines that any solution has to meet, starting with working unchanged with the VPN gateways already installed.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo that describes an existing problem and proposes guidelines for possible solutions. It fixes no protocol and proposes no mechanism.

today: RFC 4093 is an Informational memo published in August 2005, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes the problems of running Mobile IPv4 through IPsec-based VPN gateways and proposes guidelines for evaluating solutions, without specifying a mechanism of its own.

sections.title: The Problem and the Goal
sections.content:
Mobile IP agents are being deployed in enterprise networks to enable mobility across wired and wireless LANs while roaming inside the enterprise Intranet. With the growing deployment of IEEE 802.11 access points in public places such as hotels, airports and convention centres, and with wireless WAN data networks such as GPRS, the need is increasing for enabling mobile users to maintain their transport connections and constant reachability while connecting back to their target home networks protected by VPN technology. This implies that Mobile IP and VPN technologies have to coexist and function together in order to provide mobility and security to enterprise mobile users.

The memo states four goals: to identify and describe practical deployment scenarios for Mobile IP and VPN in enterprise and operator environments; to identify example usage scenarios for remote users roaming outside the home network protected by a VPN gateway; to articulate the problems resulting from Mobile IP and VPN coexistence; and to specify a set of framework guidelines to evaluate proposed solutions for supporting multi-vendor seamless IPv4 mobility across IPsec-based VPN gateways.

Access to the Intranet is typically guarded by both a firewall and a VPN device, and the Intranet can only be accessed by respecting the security policies in both. When Mobile IP is deployed in a corporate Intranet, also called a VPN domain, roaming between the Intranet, that is the trusted domain, and the Internet, the untrusted domain, becomes problematic. It would be desirable to have seamless session mobility between the two domains, because Mobile IP was designed for session mobility regardless of the network point of attachment. The current Mobile IP standards fall short of that promise for an important customer segment: corporate users who use VPN for remote access and want mobility as well, because they need continuous access to Intranet resources while roaming outside the Intranet from one subnet to another, or between the VPN domain and the Internet.

From the beginning, one explicitly stated restriction was that installed firewalls and VPN gateways had to be kept unchanged, rather than replaced or upgraded, because they had much wider deployments than Mobile IP at the time of writing. Any solution therefore needs to minimize the impact on existing VPN and firewall deployments, related standards, and de facto standards.

The memo's vocabulary is worth stating. MIPv4 is Mobile IP for IPv4 and MIPv6 is Mobile IP for IPv6. A VPN Domain is an Intranet protected by a VPN gateway. A DMZ is a small network inserted as a neutral zone between a company's private network and the outside public network, to prevent outside users from getting direct access to the private network. A Home Network is a network, possibly virtual, with a network prefix matching that of a mobile node's home address. A Home Agent is a router on a mobile node's home network that tunnels datagrams for delivery to the mobile node when it is away from home, and maintains current location information for it. An MN is a mobile node running both Mobile IP and IPsec-based VPN client software. MIPv4 inside IPsec-ESP tunnel means that Mobile IP packets are encapsulated in an IPsec-ESP tunnel established between the mobile node and the VPN gateway. IPsec-ESP inside MIPv4 tunnel means that IPsec-ESP packets are encapsulated in a Mobile IP tunnel established between the mobile node and the home agent.
sections.plainLanguage: The situation is a laptop that belongs to a company, is somewhere public, and needs to reach the company's own network. The company protects that network with a VPN, so the laptop has to encrypt everything it sends. The trouble is that the machines in between, including the ones that hand the laptop over to a different network, need to read the Mobile IP signalling to pass it on.

sections.title: Five Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The memo describes a set of deployment scenarios in which Mobile IP agents and VPN gateways have to coexist to provide mobility and security. The topology in the diagrams is an Intranet connected to the public network, where the Intranet is a private network, where private addresses are typically used, protected by a VPN gateway and perhaps by a layer-3 transparent or non-transparent firewall. When private addresses are used, the non-transparent firewall also functions as a Network Address Translator or Network Address Port Translator bridging between the two address realms. Firewalls may be placed on either side of the VPN gateway, and are referred to as inner and outer firewalls; the inner and outer firewalls typically inspect outbound and inbound traffic respectively. When a firewall is present, it MUST be configured to allow Mobile IP traffic, both control and tunneled data packets, to go through. The memo has purposely omitted firewalls from the scenarios to keep things simple. It is assumed that encryption is not enforced inside the VPN domain, because the VPN domain is viewed as a trusted network, and because it is a common VPN deployment practice to use the VPN to guard Intranet resources from unauthorized users attached to an untrusted network.

Scenario 2.1: home agents inside the Intranet, behind the VPN gateway. The home agents are deployed inside the Intranet and are not directly reachable by the mobile nodes outside it. Direct application of the Mobile IP standards works to give mobility to users inside the Intranet, but mobile users outside the Intranet can only reach the Intranet resources, including the Mobile IP agents, through the VPN gateway, which allows only authenticated IPsec traffic inside. That means the Mobile IP traffic has to run inside IPsec, which leads to two distinct problems, articulated in section 4. The memo notes that this scenario may not be common yet, but it is practical and becoming important as the need to give corporate remote users continuous access to their Intranet resources grows.

Scenario 2.2: home agent on the VPN domain border, with the gateway. The home agent is deployed on the VPN domain border, for example in the DMZ, together with the VPN gateway, and is directly reachable by mobile nodes inside or outside the Intranet. In deployments where the security policy prohibits direct communication between the roaming mobile node and outside machines, the home agent can be configured to forward only encrypted traffic. The home agent has a public interface connected to the Internet and a private interface attached to the Intranet. Mobile users will most likely have a virtual home network associated with the private interface, so that they are always away from home and always registered with the home agent. Where the gateway and the home agent are placed in a corporate DMZ, Mobile IP traffic always has to be routed through the DMZ, whether the mobile nodes are inside or outside the Intranet, which may not be acceptable to IT departments in large corporations. The scenario works in two configurations. The MIPv4-inside-IPsec-ESP arrangement has the same problems as scenario 2.1. The IPsec-ESP-inside-MIPv4 arrangement does not have those problems, but it requires some modifications to the routing logic of the home agent or the VPN gateway.

Scenario 2.3: the home agent and the VPN gateway on the same machine. This is like scenario 2.2, with the gateway and the home agent running on the same physical machine. Running both on one machine resolves the routing-related issues of scenario 2.2 when the IPsec-ESP-inside-MIPv4 configuration is used. It does not promote multi-vendor interoperability in environments where the home agent and VPN technologies must be acquired from different vendors.

Scenario 2.4: home agents outside the VPN domain. The home agents are deployed outside the Intranet, for example in an operator network. The IPsec tunnel endpoints are the mobile node and the VPN gateway, and the home network will most likely be a virtual home network located at the home agent, through which authorized remote users can reach the corporate Intranet and keep their transport session connectivity while roaming. This scenario does not support mobility inside the Intranet. It is most practical to run IPsec-ESP inside a Mobile IP tunnel, so that the mobile node and the home agent are the tunnel endpoints and the IPsec-ESP packet from the mobile node to the VPN gateway is encapsulated in the Mobile IP tunnel. That is because the mobile nodes can register with the home agent without establishing an IPsec tunnel to the VPN gateway.

Scenario 2.5: the home agent and the VPN gateway on the local link. This is like scenario 2.3, with the gateway and home agent sitting on the local link, most naturally co-located in the same box although that is not a requirement. The combined device is assumed to be reachable from the external network, so it has a public IP address, and the firewall is assumed to be configured to allow direct access to it. This deployment works today without any technical problems with IPsec-ESP running inside a Mobile IP tunnel. Running Mobile IP inside the IPsec-ESP tunnel would give the same problems as scenario 2.1, so it is deployed with IPsec-ESP running inside the Mobile IP tunnel. It is not practical for large deployments, on the order of thousands of users, because of the large and distributed security perimeter.
sections.plainLanguage: Where the home agent sits decides everything. Inside the corporate network it cannot be reached from a hotel; on the border it can; outside the corporate network entirely it can, but then roaming inside the office no longer works. Putting it in the same box as the VPN gateway avoids the routing trouble but ties the two products together.

sections.title: What Breaks, and Where
sections.content:
The five scenarios were evaluated against two criteria: whether the scenario is common and practical, and whether it reveals any problems resulting from Mobile IP and VPN coexistence. The authors believe that scenario 2.1 is the most important and practical one, because of the rising need to give corporate remote users continuous access to their Intranet resources. After analyzing each scenario, the memo concludes that the problems occurring in scenarios 2.2 and 2.4 are either the same as those in scenario 2.1 or a subset of them, so solving scenario 2.1 solves those too. The scenarios in 2.3 and 2.5 do not introduce functional problems resulting from coexistence, and so there is no need to seek a solution for them.

The problem statement section then describes the roaming scenarios corresponding to scenario 2.1, where a mobile node needs continuous access to the Intranet resources regardless of whether it is roaming inside or outside the Intranet. The scenarios are built on a multi-subnetted Mobile IP-enabled Intranet protected by an IPsec-based VPN gateway. The Intranet may include both wired and IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN deployments, and it is also possible to see IEEE 802.11 deployments outside the Intranet because of the perceived lack of current 802.11 security.

Registering in co-located mode. Here the IPsec tunnel endpoints are at the mobile node and the VPN gateway, which results in the Mobile IP tunnel from the mobile node to the home agent being encapsulated inside the IPsec tunnel. The mobile node obtains an address at its point of attachment, by DHCP or some other means, and then sets up an IPsec tunnel to the VPN gateway, after which it can register with its home agent through that tunnel. The IPsec tunnel security association is identified by a triplet consisting of the Security Parameter Index, the mobile node's IP destination address, and the security protocol identifier, whether AH or ESP. That means that as the mobile node's IP destination address changes on each IP subnet handoff, the IPsec tunnel has to be re-established. The memo says this could have noticeable performance implications on real-time applications and in resource-constrained wireless networks, and that in effect there is no mobility support for the tunnel endpoint changes associated with the mobile node's movements.

Registering via a foreign agent. Where a mobile node is in a network where mobility support is provided through a foreign agent, and no DHCP-allocated address and co-located mode is possible, the memo says severe trouble results. When the mobile node arrives at the visited network, it has to reach the foreign agent with registration requests so that the foreign agent can send them on to the home agent. The mobile node will most likely not be able to register with the foreign agent, because the registration requests are sent encrypted and the foreign agent cannot decrypt them. If the mobile node had a policy allowing split tunneling, so that it could reach the foreign agent with clear text messages, the foreign agent would still not get through the VPN gateway unless the home agent is reachable from outside and the Intranet security policy allows Mobile IP registration packets to bypass the VPN gateway. Even if the home agent is reachable and the registration succeeds, the foreign agent, which is likely in a different administrative domain, will not be able to relay packets between the mobile node and the VPN gateway. Packets from the mobile node are encapsulated by the foreign agent with IP-in-IP, which the VPN gateway drops, and packets from the VPN gateway carry ESP payloads with IP-in-IP inside, which the foreign agent drops, because it expects IP-in-IP-encapsulated traffic to the mobile node.

The use of a trusted foreign agent has also been suggested, meaning one that is really a combined VPN gateway and foreign agent. The scenario works fine in that case, because the tunnel endpoints are at the foreign agent and the VPN gateway. But it cannot be expected that the foreign agent in access networks such as wireless hot spots or CDMA 2000 networks will have security associations with any given corporate network, so this is not particularly realistic in the general mobility case. It would also leave the traffic between the foreign agent and the mobile node unprotected, which is clearly undesirable on a wireless link.

The summary. A mobile node roaming outside the Intranet has to establish an IPsec tunnel to its home VPN gateway first, in order to register with its home agent, because it cannot reach the home agent inside the private protected network directly from outside. That forces the Mobile IP traffic from the mobile node to a node inside the Intranet to run inside an IPsec tunnel, so it is not in the clear, and that leads to two distinct problems. In co-located mode, the IPsec tunnel has to be re-established on each IP subnet handoff, with performance implications for real-time applications and resource-constrained wireless networks. In non-co-located mode, using a foreign agent care-of address, the problem becomes severe: the mobile node may be unable to register with its home agent through the foreign agent at all, because the foreign agent cannot understand Mobile IP registration requests that are encrypted in the IPsec tunnel. Even if the mobile node could reach the foreign agent with unencrypted registration requests and those requests could pass through the VPN gateway, there would still be a problem routing data packets, because the VPN will not allow IP-in-IP-encapsulated packets from the foreign agent through, and the ESP-encapsulated packets from the VPN gateway to the mobile node will be dropped by the foreign agent, which expects IP-in-IP-encapsulated traffic to the mobile node.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things go wrong. If the laptop registers directly, the encrypted tunnel has to be rebuilt every time it moves to a new network, which costs time and radio. If it registers through a foreign agent, the messages cannot get through at all, because the agent cannot read the encrypted registration and the two ends of the path each discard the other's packets.

sections.title: Guidelines for a Solution
sections.content:
The memo lists ten guidelines that a solution for Mobile IP traversal across VPN gateways should meet.

On preservation of existing VPN infrastructure, the solution MUST work with currently deployed VPN gateways. The memo calls this the whole reason for the investigation: finding a way to deploy Mobile IP where a VPN solution is already in place. On software upgrades to existing VPN clients and gateways, the solution SHOULD minimize changes to existing software. On the IPsec protocol, the solution SHOULD NOT require any changes to existing IPsec or key-exchange standard protocols implemented by VPN gateways, and SHOULD NOT require that the VPN gateway or the VPN client implement any new protocols in addition to the existing standard protocols.

On multi-vendor interoperability, the solution MUST provide it, whereby the Mobile IP mobility agents, the mobility clients, the VPN server and the VPN client solutions may come from four different vendors. This is typical for medium and large enterprises that buy and deploy best-of-breed multi-vendor solutions for IP routing, VPNs and firewalls. On the Mobile IP protocol, the solution MUST adhere to it, meaning it MUST NOT impose any changes that violate the Mobile IP protocol. It MAY introduce new extensions to Mobile IP nodes per the guidelines in the Mobile IP protocol, but to overcome barriers to deployment it is highly desirable to avoid any changes to Mobile IP mobility agents such as the foreign agent and the home agent. The solution MAY require more than one instance of Mobile IP running in parallel, which the memo calls multiple encapsulation.

On handoff overhead, it is imperative to keep key management overhead down to a minimum in order to support fast handoffs across IP subnets, so the solution MUST propose a mechanism to avoid or minimize IPsec tunnel security association renegotiation and IKE renegotiation as the mobile node changes its point of network attachment. On scalability, availability, reliability and performance, the solution complexity MUST increase at most linearly with the number of mobile nodes registered and accessing resources inside the Intranet, and the solution MAY introduce additional header or tunnelling overhead if needed. On functional entities, the solution MAY introduce new Mobile IP-compliant functional entities.

On the implications of intervening NAT gateways, the solution MUST be able to work with the existing Mobile IP and IPsec NAT traversal solutions. On security requirements, the solution MUST provide security that is not inferior to what is already provided to existing nomadic computing remote access users, for confidentiality, authentication, message integrity, protection against replay attacks, and related security services.
sections.plainLanguage: The guidelines are mostly about not breaking what is already installed. A fix has to work with the VPN gateways companies already own, without changing IPsec or inventing new protocols, and it has to work when the pieces come from different suppliers. The one piece of new behaviour it does need is a way to move the laptop to a new network without rebuilding the encrypted tunnel from scratch.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it describes an existing problem and proposes guidelines for possible solutions, so its security implications are indirect, through the guidelines it proposes for the solutions. It points to the security requirements in section 5.10 as the relevant ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not change how anything is secured. The security it cares about is the security a future solution would have to keep, and that is set out as the last of the guidelines.

messages.label: REGISTRATION
messages.note: The registration requests are encrypted inside the IPsec tunnel, so the foreign agent cannot read the Mobile IP headers it needs in order to relay them.

messages.label: IP-IN-IP
messages.note: Packets from the mobile node are encapsulated by the foreign agent with IP-in-IP, and the VPN gateway drops them.

messages.label: ESP
messages.note: Packets from the VPN gateway carry ESP payloads with IP-in-IP inside, and the foreign agent drops them because it expects IP-in-IP-encapsulated traffic to the mobile node.

viz.caption: THE GUIDELINES A SOLUTION MUST MEET

items.title: Work with deployed gateways
items.text: The solution MUST work with currently deployed VPN gateways. This is the whole reason for the investigation.

items.title: Minimise software changes
items.text: The solution SHOULD minimize changes to existing VPN client and gateway software.

items.title: Leave IPsec alone
items.text: The solution SHOULD NOT require changes to existing IPsec or key-exchange protocols, and SHOULD NOT require the gateway or client to implement any new protocols.

items.title: Allow four vendors
items.text: The solution MUST provide multi-vendor interoperability, so the mobility agents, mobility clients, VPN server and VPN client may come from four different vendors.

items.title: Adhere to Mobile IP
items.text: The solution MUST adhere to the MIPv4 protocol, and SHOULD avoid changes to the foreign agent and home agent.

items.title: Cheap handoffs
items.text: The solution MUST propose a mechanism to avoid or minimize IPsec security association renegotiation and IKE renegotiation as the mobile node changes its point of attachment.

items.title: Scale linearly
items.text: The solution complexity MUST increase at most linearly with the number of mobile nodes registered and accessing resources inside the Intranet.

items.title: Work with NAT traversal
items.text: The solution MUST be able to work with the existing MIPv4 and IPsec NAT traversal solutions.
